newsitem.title: UK: Politicians, scientists demand N.Sea fishing curbs.
newsitem.headline: Politicians, scientists demand N.Sea fishing curbs.

text.p: Politicians, lobbyists and scientists joined forces in Britain on Thursday to demand curbs on industrial fishing in the North Sea, warning that food stocks as well as wildlife were being seriously hit by over-fishing.
Their call came with the publication of a report showing industrial fishing -- which turns fish into oil and feed -- is taking out much of the food of key species eaten by people.

"Everybody seems ready to face up to the problem except the governments," said Lord Peter Melchett, executive director of the environmental campaigning group Greenpeace in Britain. "The governments need to act now." The report, prepared by scientists funded by the Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever, said the species targeted by industrial fishing vessels were the main food source for fish like cod, haddock and whiting.
Unilever, one of the world's largest purchasers of fish, is concerned about the sustainability of stocks, a spokesman said.
It has decided to stop using oil from industrial fishing and, with the World Wide Fund for Nature, is creating an independent body to draw up responsible fishing guidelines.

Jacqueline McGlade of Warwick University in central England, one of the report's authors, told a news conference in the House of Commons a new initiative was needed involving scientists, industry and policymakers to study changes in fishing practices.

She said it was essential to get a better idea of how much fish was caught above agreed quotas and then illegally landed or dumped, adding it might be necessary to agree a line in the North Sea beyond which industrial fishing would be banned. The report was backed by Scottish members of the ruling Conservatives as well as opposition Labour and Scottish Nationalist members of parliament, together with Greenpeace and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds.

The British government is under fire from its own MPs over fishing, in particular so-called quota hopping by Spanish fishermen who have bought up British boats so they can fish under British EU quotas.
Fisheries minister Tom Baldry announced on Wednesday a 10-point plan to help the fishing industry, centered on a demand to reform the European Union's Common Fisheries Policy.
The government has also announced a new research project into the effect of industrial fishing off Scotland.
